Tax Increment Financing and TIF Area Tax Increment Financing (TIF) is a funding mechanism for redevelopment autho- rized by Chapter 163, Florida Statutes. TIF captures the incremental increase in tax revenues resulting from redevelopment and uses it to pay for public improve- ments needed to support the redevelopment program. TIF funds in Palafox have fi nanced park improvements, annual energy costs for streetlights and some operating budget costs for the CRA since 2003. Moving forward TIF will be used for the acquisition of land, support of innovative code and law enforcement ini- tiatives, demolition of deteriorated structures, site preparation, visioning studies, matching grant programs and infrastructure improvements. Authorize for execution of the 2025/2026 Financial Responsibility Agreement between Hillsborough	
County and Mosaic Fertilizer, LLC. This is an agreement renewed annually that ensures that if Mosaic	
Fertilizer, LLC, were to fail to complete reclamation of mined land in Hillsborough County that there	
would be funding available for the County to complete the reclamation work. This Financial Responsibility	
Agreement protects the County from negative financial impacts of adverse environmental issues and/or	
failure of the company to complete required reclamation activities.

The amendment was moved and seconded. CM Lahnen explained that this was a re-filing of 2024-0949, which was passed last year as part of his Council strategic priority funding. He explained that one of the projects he intended to fund saw a cost reduction from $71,000 to $53,000. Rather than submit one bill requesting a carryover and then a subsequent bill approving a grant sheet change, he allowed the funding to go to the reserves, and this bill appropriates the funds from reserves for the project at the reduced amount. He explained that the substance of the agreement had not changed. 

Mr. Peterson explained the amendment. 

CM Salem asked whether CM Lahnen had plans for the remaining $20,000 resulting from the project cost reduction. CM Lahnen said it would go to the General Fund. 

CM Clark-Murray restated the bill's premise and asked whether her understanding was correct. CM Lahnen reiterated the rationale for filing this bill now rather than two bills earlier. 

The amendment was approved unanimously.

• Discussion on Council Strategic Priorities
Council President Carrico talked about strategic initiative funding for the next budget cycle, roughly $10 million. There was a discussion about the process by which council priorities are identified.  In previous years, a council workshop was conducted to select common priorities, and there were also years wherein council members chose projects/programs to fund through strategic initiative funds.  The Council President recommended that for Fiscal Year 2026-2027 the council request the Mayor place the annual strategic plan budget appropriation ($10,019,591) into a designated contingency account for the council to address various City and council priorities during the Finance Committee and city council budget deliberations.

Mr. Everett asked the panel how they would define the difference between a capital project and asset-based investments. Daryl Joseph of the Parks Department said his department classifies items by cost, noting that anything over $100,000 is usually considered a capital investment. He said the purchase of equipment, like furniture, would be considered an asset-based investment. Nina Sickler of the Public Works Department said they consider the useful life of something when classifying it as either a capital or asset-based investment, noting that a capital investment will be safe and usable for 30 or more years. Robert Waremburg from the Procurement Division said that, with capital investments, consideration should be given to whether they entail construction or professional design services, as there are laws and procedures that must be followed when selecting architects and engineers.

CM Arias asked if projects funded must be opened to public use. Mr. Waremburg said it depended on whether the City owns the property. Mr. Joseph said that any dollars put into a facility by the City, regardless of ownership, would be associated with public use. He added that, with privately owned facilities, a joint-use agreement may be required once City funds are accepted.

Tyler Nolen, Special Projects Coordinator for Northeast Florida Regional Council (NEFRC), presented on the NEFRC’s support of the City of Jacksonville Public Safety.  He stated that NEFRC provides funds to public safety entities. One example of this was the Local Emergency Planning Committee for Hazardous Materials (LEPC), which is required in every state by the federal government. He added that the Florida Statutes require these committees to focus strictly on hazardous materials. He said they also have the Region 3 Healthcare Coalition, which he described as the emergency-preparedness sector of healthcare. NEFRC, in general, can provide support to fire and rescue, sheriff’s offices, and emergency management offices upon request. 

Mr. Nolen provided an overview of LEPCs and explained that they were created by the Superfund Amendment and Reauthorization Act of 1986 in response to a series of disasters in the 1980s. In Florida, the Division of Emergency Management pushes contracts to all regional councils to implement the program and support hazardous materials teams. He added that there are three hazardous material teams in Northeast Florida. He continued, stating that JFRD was so large that Jacksonville, in effect, had two type one hazardous material teams in the City. He defined type one teams as those with the means to respond to any incident regardless of any chemical or radiological components. Because of this, the Florida Division of Emergency Management updated its

The amendment was moved and seconded. Mr. Peterson explained the amendment. CM Boylan asked if the funds were available to all Council Members. Mr. Peterson said there were several funding sources, including the Solid Waste Class III Mitigation Fund, into which 50 cents per ton of waste is deposited. He said that money from those funds must be spent within a seven-mile radius of the waste management facility. He explained that the Cardroom Tax account receives state funds related to the Best Bet cardroom on Monument Road, and that the funds must be spent on parks within a five-mile radius of the facility. The Autumn Bonds Investment Pool Earnings can be used on any Capital Improvement Project. The amendment was moved and seconded. 
Ms. Reber explained the amendment.
The amendment was unanimously approved.

CM Salem asked Mr. Jeffrey whether there is a maximum one can receive from the down payment assistance program. Mr. Jeffrey stated that there are two different programs: the Headstart to Homeownership program, which provides up to $25,000, and a new program created last year for single-family construction that will build new homes for individuals at 50% or lower AMI. 

CM Salem asked whether any of these programs require repayment of the down payment assistance. Mr. Jeffrey stated that they are all deferred payments, and that as long as one stays in the home, a lien of 5, 10, or 15 years is placed on the property depending on the amount of funding received. He added that if a homeowner stays in the property for 15 years the lien goes away, and that if a homeowner either sells the property or moves out and rents it out, a prorated amount is repaid.

She said that CM Salem previously added an amendment to that bill to add another floor of 17 percent of General Fund revenues. She said that as they go through the audit, they determine whether there are any unfunded incentive obligations and, if so, what the balance is. They then determine if any excess revenues after expenses would be committed above those floor amounts. 2026-213 requires that, while they were disclosing that commitment in the audit report, a piece of legislation be introduced and passed to move those funds.

Mr. A.J. Souto, JEA Treasurer, provided an overview of the bill. He explained that prior to 2023, JEA would approach its board and subsequently the City Council on an as-needed basis for authorization to issue debt, which resulted in a patchwork of authorizations dating to 1988 for the electric system and 1997 for the water and sewer system. He added that the patchwork of authorizations made it difficult to track, difficult to provide transparency, and difficult to answer how much outstanding debt JEA has and how much it is allowed to have outstanding.

Mr. Souto then explained that in 2023, he and his predecessor proposed Ordinance 2023-724 to formally establish not-to-exceed debt outstanding amounts for each of JEA's systems: $1.9 billion for the electric system, $2.5 billion for the water and sewer system, and $150 million for the district energy system, also referred to as the chilled water system. He added that JEA pledged to the City Council that it would submit a one-page summary with its annual budget to prove compliance with the not-to-exceed debt outstanding limit while enhancing transparency. 

Mr. Souto stated that in June 2026, JEA requested a further increase to its not-to-exceed debt outstanding amounts for each system. He added that since 2023, JEA has executed three transactions, has just closed on two bond transactions for fiscal year 2026, one for the electric system and one for the water and sewer system, and is looking at its planned bond transactions

Professor Carney explained that a digital twin is a living digital model of a city, including its buildings, infrastructure, environmental systems, and transportation, that allows people to visualize relationships and make better decisions. He stated that the team had been working on Jacksonville’s digital twin for three years, examining the city’s growth and whether the City is prepared to handle that growth given challenges such as inadequate public transportation, traffic congestion, and flooding.

He explained that the JaxTwin platform pulls together data from a wide range of sources, including transportation, the physical environment, topography, bathymetry, sea levels, flood and storm surges, housing, and demographics. He added that the platform turns that data into a legible graphic interface.

Dr. Chen then presented an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) system developed in partnership with JTA, explaining that it has two goals: serving people without cars, impoverished people, and people with disabilities, and improving transit on-time performance. He added that the AI agent evaluates these goals and generates recommendations to improve the performance of the transit system.

Mr. Jon Michael Barker, FIND Subcommittee Chair, stated that the Subcommittee met the previous day, and invited Mr. Brian Burket, Parks Department, to report the Subcommittee’s recommendations to the Commission.

Mr. Burket explained that FIND is the agency that oversees maintenance of the Intracoastal Waterway in twelve counties along the Atlantic coast. He added that a portion of ad valorem taxes goes to FIND for maintenance of the channel and for a grant program to which local governments can apply for projects that improve access to rivers and waterways. Mr. Burket explained that the Subcommittee recommended four projects with a combined project value of just over $7 million. 

He noted that the FIND Board sets a target cap for each county that typically rises about $100,000 each year. He stated that the City was awarded around $3 million last year, and that this year the City requested $3.3 million. He explained that the City’s requests go slightly beyond the target cap, but that the City was advised by its local FIND Board Commissioner to be a little more aggressive.

Mr. Burket explained that last year, the City received grant funding for Phase 1 of the Sisters Creek Transient Facilities project, which went toward the bathhouse. He explained that Phase 2 was too expensive to include in last year’s request, so the City is requesting funding this year for 500 feet of new transient docks as a continuation project. The Auditor’s recommended amendment was moved and seconded. Ms. Reber explained the amendment. The amendment was approved unanimously. 

Chair Miller said there was another amendment and invited Jerry Holland, Supervisor of Elections, to explain the amendment. First, he said there were two methods for post-election audits. The current method is a hand-counted audit of a randomly selected race and precincts chosen by the Canvassing Board and county judge. He said the second method utilizes technology called Clear Ballot, which takes a picture of each oval on every ballot and audits 100 percent of ballots. He said the equipment was separate from the machines used to tabulate votes. He said 32 of Florida’s 67 counties have adopted the technology, using county funding. Mr. Holland said the State wants all counties to use this technology and has provided funding for counties to purchase it by the end of the year. This bill would appropriate state funds to purchase the equipment. He said the amendment would identify the company as Clear Ballot, which is the only company certified to do post-election audits in the state. 

The amendment was moved and seconded. 

Ms. Staffopoulos clarified that the amendment would add language to the bill for a direct contract with Clear Ballot that would be authorized under Section 126.108(g) of the Ordinance Code, which would provide an exemption from competitive solicitation.

• Amends Ch. 651 (Expedited Permitting) to revise the eligibility criteria for the expedited permitting process, designate the Public Works Department as responsible for coordination and implementation, and establish fees
• Establishes an initial Expedited Permitting Program Fee of $20,000, which may be increased up to $40,000 by the Director of Public Works without Council approval
• Establishes an Exceptional Project Fee, which cannot exceed 200% of the Expedited Permitting Program Fee without approval of the Chief Administrative Officer, for projects based on size, complexity, number of structures or permits, number of required reviewing agencies, phased permitting requirements, or other characteristics requiring greater resources, to be paid in addition to the Expedited Permitting Program Fee
• These fees are supplemental and will not replace, reduce, credit against, or otherwise affect any other fees that are applicable to any project
• The Expedited Permitting Program Fee and Exceptional Project Fee will be deposited as follows: 90% to the Building Inspection Fund and 10% to the Affordable Housing Special Revenue Fund

The elevated platform would be approximately five feet above existing grade, with a total height of approximately 12.85 feet, including the backup generator, to meet flood elevation requirements.
